question: What is the Islamic punishment for rape, and is the victim ever to blame?
asked: There's a lot of talk right now about a recent, particularly vicious case of rape in a particular country: a lady ran out of gas, and as she was waiting for help, some men came and sexually assaulted her in front of her children. There's a lot of talk amongst the scholars, the laity and the politicians. What is the Islamic punishment for rape, and can the perpetrators be made an example of? A lot of people are also talking about whose fault it is, and blame is sometimes even being assigned to the victim. What does the Shari'ah say about all of this?
answer:
Now, obviously, I've given you the trigger warning: this is going to be a very explicit response, so keep this point in mind. Also, I did not mention the name of the country, because what concerns us is the Islamic... well, what concerns me in this Q&A. Obviously I'm not living in that country; I don't have the right to speak specifically about the cultural context of what is going on. But I will speak generically from a religious perspective.

And there is no question that one of the primary goals of the Shari'ah is the protection of family and the protection of honor. And that is why, in order to protect the family and to protect honor, the Shari'ah has revealed so many laws. One of the fundamental five goals of Islamic law is to protect honor and to protect nasl, or family. And that is why marriage has been legislated, and all other avenues that are outside of marriage, all other avenues to satisfy one's desires, have been criminalized and penalized. And there are severe punishments, especially for the crime of rape.

And in fact, there is a hadith to this effect as well. There are a number of traditions found, and again, there are multiple versions; I'll summarize for you what is, inshallah, the most authentic version. It is mentioned in Sunan Abu Dawud and other books that a lady was going for Fajr to the masjid in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and a man overpowered her and raped her. And when she managed to basically push him off or whatnot, or after the act was over, she began shouting and yelling that she had been assaulted. And people went to try to find the person; a group of Muhajirun went to look for this person. And she complained to the Prophet ﷺ as well that she had been assaulted. Then a person was brought to the masjid: the group that had been sent to find somebody found a lone person who seemed guilty, and they brought him. And initially she said, "Yes, that is the man." But as the Prophet continued to interrogate, and the news spread that there had been a rape, another man confessed and said, "I did it, ya Rasulallah." So the first man was let go, and he was apologized to: "We're sorry, we got the wrong person," basically. And the second man, it was ordered that he be executed. And the Prophet spoke kindly to the woman and basically let her go, and said, "You are not sinful."

Now, this incident is actually very profound for us in terms of the lessons that we can derive from it. A number of things.

Realize that these crimes occur in every society. I mean, even in prophetic Medina, even in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, where society is a role-model society, where everybody's iman is the highest in human history, you still have some scum. You still have the worst of the worst. You still have criminals. You see, you can never eradicate criminality from the hearts of a people in a society. You can strive, you can build a prophetic Medina, but you cannot enforce that level of piety on every single person. And no matter what society does, there's always going to be criminals and murderers and thieves and rapists. You're always going to get the dregs and the sludge and the lowest of the low, the scum of the earth. There's only so much that laws can do, and that the iman you preach to the members can do.

I mean, we understand this point. In the Medina of the Prophet ﷺ, where the Prophet ﷺ is giving the khutbah every week, where Abu Bakr and 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali radiyallahu 'anhum, where all of the Sahabah you've ever heard of are living in that city, in that city this crime occurs. So subhanAllah, there is evil everywhere. There was even evil in the city of the Prophet ﷺ in that timeframe. There's only so much that laws can do. In the end, every person has to preach and teach. Every person has to do whatever he or she can.

Also realize that this is prophetic Medina, and so everybody is acting in a professional manner publicly; everybody's dressed in a professional Islamic manner. Still this deed occurred. So again, we have to be very clear here. While it is true that Islam mandates dress codes on men and on women, and while it is true that that is an important aspect of our morality, to claim that if everybody dressed in a certain manner, rape would not occur: what do we say to this incident here? Despite the fact that everybody is dressed according to prophetic standards, the way that they should be. And they should, by the way; I'm not saying that we should neglect that. Of course we should encourage modesty, encourage a proper dress code. But no matter how we do that, it's not going to change that there's going to be scum, there's going to be evil people, there's going to be people with a disease in their heart. So this is another point that we need to be explicit about.

Yet a third point that we can be explicit about is that the lady was walking to Fajr alone. She didn't have any person with her. And she cried out that she had been assaulted, and people came and went, and search parties were sent, and she went to the Prophet ﷺ. None of the Sahabah reproached her. None of them said, "What were you doing outside?" None of them said, "Why did you leave your house?" She was going for a legitimate reason. It's not her fault; she's going to pray Fajr, and she's going in the city of Medina. How can she be blamed for going about her daily business?

So to assign blame on somebody who's not doing anything wrong, and to make them feel, a'udhu billah, guilty or responsible for a crime that they have nothing to do with, a'udhu billah, you are causing PTSD, you're causing shock, you're causing an extra layer of guilt for absolutely no reason. The Prophet did not tell the lady, "What were you doing outside alone?" None of the Sahabah said to her, "Why were you walking to the masjid alone?" It's a legitimate reason, and she's in her city. It's a safe place, and she had every right to do what she was doing.

Yet another important point that we have to stress here, and again, this is a very frank talk here, is that this lady, obviously, understandably, is traumatized. And the first man that is brought, she says, "Yes, that's him." I mean, it was dark, it was pre-Fajr; she's not 100% certain. And so the first person she sees that the Muhajirun brought... they found one man wandering around in the vicinity, and they dragged him to the masjid. He's protesting, "What do you mean? I didn't do anything, I was here." And initially suspicion is on him. And even the lady (again, innocent, it's not her fault) assumes, "Yes, that is that person, it was him." And so the interrogation is increased: "Why did you do this?" We're trying to extract evidence.

Because obviously this is a very, very sensitive point here, and I want you to understand this point. Wallahi, we understand that, generally speaking, when a lady says that she has been assaulted, she is telling the truth. No one wants to lie about this. But at the same time, when she identifies the culprit, when she says who it is, and in the circumstances of this type of hadith, where it's dark and whatnot, how can we be 100% certain? We have to be careful here that there must be some evidence beyond just one person versus one person. If we were to open this door, everybody can accuse anybody of any crime. And so this is a very, very difficult issue, because neither do we want to put the onus of proof on an innocent victim, nor do we want to make somebody who's innocent a victim as well.

Here in this hadith, we see that an innocent man was dragged in front of the Prophet ﷺ. The Sahabah are getting irritated, because they're certain it's him, because she says it's him. And it's not her fault, because it was dark and she's traumatized and whatever; she might have had in her mind... so she sees that person.

And by the way, in America, how many times, and especially when the ethnicities are different (do your research in this regard), how many times has a lady sworn under oath that that man did it, and she is certain that it is that man, but it turns out five, 10, 20, 50 years later, DNA comes and she finds out: no, it wasn't him, it was somebody else. SubhanAllah. You cannot base a guilty verdict just on the memory or recollection of one person, no matter how...

And this is why it is so important that we believe in the Akhirah, because justice sometimes is not served in this world. And I speak directly to all victims of abuse: try to get your justice in this world. You have every right to try. In case you don't get it, subhanAllah, you have the Akhirah, and you will get ultimate justice. And Allah 'azza wa jall will give the mazlum every single reward that is coming to them, and will punish the dhalim according to the level that they deserve to be punished.

We also see from this incident another important point. There is this notion that unfortunately is taught in some societies, and that is that we should not publicize these crimes: that the victim should be quiet and save the honor of the guilty party. That the victim should not shame the guilty party, especially if the guilty party is a friend, a family friend, an uncle, a relative, something of this nature; she should protect the honor of the person. And to this we respond: here we have the lady screaming and yelling and saying this happened, and calling for punishment. And nobody said to her, "Oh, you have to protect the honor of the criminal."

The criminal has no honor to protect. The rapist has no dignity that you should shelter him with. There is absolutely no problem in exposing the crime of a predator. And the one who has been a victim has every right to accuse the one who has victimized or oppressed or molested or done anything, she or he. Because again, let's be honest here, it's not just women; men and children also get molested and sexually abused in this regard. It is 100% Islamic, 100% Islamic, that the victim of these crimes is explicit about the one who has done this.

Now, this is where it gets a little bit problematic: third parties, and should they say anything or not. And we say: third parties, if you have nothing to do with the case, if you don't know... Now, what do I mean by this? You have a person and another person; both of them are accusing each other: "You're lying," or "You did this and that." If you are involved, and you are in the relationship of one of these two, and you know the story, in this case you have every right to get involved and defend or accuse or whatnot. But if you are watching from a distance, if you're watching online, if you're seeing things from afar, in this case we have to remember the hadith of the famous incident of the slander of 'A'ishah. When somebody accused, a'udhu billah, a'udhu billah, our mother 'A'ishah radiyallahu 'anha, Allah says in the Qur'an: why did you have to speak? Why did you have to say anything? If you're not involved, be quiet. If you're not involved, it's not your business, and let justice take its course.

But the victim goes to the court. In this case, she went to the Prophet ﷺ. In any society or land, she or he should go to the police; go and present your evidence. And the other person comes and defends and whatnot. That's their business. Third parties, when it comes to specific people accusing each other: if you don't know, then you really don't know. Unless there's evidence, unless the court has ruled, in this case, be quiet. If each one of them is negating or accusing, and it's not clear which one is telling the truth, they're both your Muslim brother or sister. In this case, it's not your business to really get involved, unless certainty is reached, unless the trial is taking place and it is clear who the guilty party is.

So again, we have to differentiate. Why do I say this? Because all too often, social media itself becomes a circus and drama. All too often, tattletaling and gossip and innuendo and slander make the situation much worse than it needs to be. And if you do not know what happened, then be quiet. If you're not involved, be quiet. If you are involved, then no problem: speak your mind, no problem; say what needs to be said, no problem; be an alibi or talk about evidence. That is exactly the difference between those that are directly involved in the case (and for them there is no silence; go ahead and speak what needs to be done and take it to justice) versus those that are not involved in the case. So this is also a point that we derive from this issue.

Also, another point that we derive is that our Prophet ﷺ spoke gentle words to the lady and let her go. And this clearly indicates, and obviously it's common sense, that the victim is not guilty. The victim is not guilty in this regard. If something of this nature has happened, nobody should feel that it was their fault. This is one of the common psychological issues: especially youngsters and especially vulnerable people begin to think, "Maybe I did something, maybe I said something, maybe I sat in a certain manner." Dear brother or sister, dear child, dear victim of molestation: it is never, ever your fault. You did not do anything to justify whatever happened to you. Anybody who did something to you, that is something they have to answer for in front of Allah. You should never feel any type of guilt if you are not guilty, for the perpetrator doing something against you. So don't let Shaytan come to you and start working in your mind in this regard.

Now, also we have to realize as well... now, this is again a very sensitive topic here, because I just said that this is prophetic Medina, I just said everybody's acting in accordance with the Shari'ah, I just said everybody's dressed in accordance with Islam. Now I'm going to say something that I need people to pay attention to. You can have two separate and distinct issues, both of which are equally valid. They're not mutually exclusive.

It doesn't matter what is going on around you. It doesn't matter how somebody dresses. It doesn't matter what is going on. **The rapist is 100% guilty for the rape.** The criminal is 100% guilty for the crime. The one who steals, the thief, the murderer: all of them bear 100% responsibility. That's all there.

That having been said, we as individuals are also obliged to do whatever we can, whatever is reasonable, knowing that we can take all the precautions and still something can happen. You can lock all your doors and set up all of your security alarms, and still somebody can break into your house and steal. You can be very careful as you're walking down the street and make sure that your wallet is in a particular place and whatnot; still a pickpocket can come and find it and pickpocket you. Still, that doesn't negate the fact that you try to be wise and you try to be sensible. The two are not mutually exclusive.

And this is where it gets sensitive, because when I say, for example, that one should take reasonable precautions, the immediate response is, "Oh, you're victim-shaming." No, I am not, not at all. As I said, you can take all the reasonable precautions and still something can happen. Now, again, I'm not talking about this particular case. To me, it appears that there was nothing unreasonable, but again, I wasn't there, and I don't know the whole details. I'm speaking generically; I'm not speaking about this one case here. And so there is no doubt that the more precautions that you take in a reasonable society, the better it is.

And we also have to point out the vulgarity and the indecency that is now predominant across the globe. It is very true to point out that this type of violence that we are seeing... again, we're not exonerating; it's 100% the rapist's fault. But the overt sexualization that is happening across the globe, across the globe, in Hollywood, in Bollywood, in Lollywood, in every single society; the pornography that is rampant... And again, it's an awkward thing to say, brothers and sisters, but do you know that of the top 10 countries in the world in terms of pornography, I believe five of them are Muslim countries? I think it was a Pew survey or something like that: of the top 10 countries in the world that, a'udhu billah, search this type of stuff, five are from Muslim lands. You don't think that's going to have an impact?

Now, again, I'm not saying there's an exoneration. A'udhu billah, it doesn't matter how somebody dresses. It doesn't matter what the man has seen. It doesn't matter what's going on. In the end of the day, the rapist is guilty. In the end of the day, if a man feels an inclination, he has to deal with it, and he has to take care of it in a halal manner. He is not allowed to just go and do whatever he wants. Still, as a society, we need to ask ourselves: what are we doing? Is this healthy? Is this normal? As a society, we have to have very frank conversations in this regard: is it good for society to allow pornography? Is it good to allow the objectification of women?

The two are separate. It doesn't matter how much you objectify women; it does not give one allowance, one millimeter of an allowance, for the rapist. Still, as I said, you lock your doors and you take precautions, and then you put your trust in Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, and it's still possible you can be robbed. Similarly, we do our job as much as we can, and we act in a manner that is Islamic and decent: our interactions with the opposite gender, our dress code, our societal norms, decency. It is there, yes indeed, but even if you have it, you can still be raped, as happened in Medina. My point is that those precautions, generally speaking, will minimize, yes, but they will not eliminate. Those precautions will help society, but they will not eliminate 100%.

And it is an awkward reality, and I speak here now especially to the men that are listening. And I want to say something again, very, very frank, over here. I want you to have a very awkward conversation with your loved ones, your female relatives: your sisters, your wives, if you're able to (because again, it depends from culture to culture), even your adult daughters, or your aunts or whatnot, if you're able to, because again, this all goes back to your haya and whatnot. But definitely your wives and your sisters that you're able to speak with: ask them a very, very blunt question: "Have you ever been in any way, fashion or form molested?" And you will be shocked. Because survey after survey has shown that the statistics of being molested or catcalled or groped, especially in Muslim lands, are beyond belief.

One survey which I read, actually: I saw the United Nations website, and they have a survey in many, many countries. In one Muslim land (I'm not going to mention which one, but it is predominantly Muslim; some of the greatest 'ulama of the world live there and whatnot), in one Muslim land, they said 99% of the women they surveyed, 99%, had been in some fashion or form molested. By molestation we mean groping, in the crowd somebody does something; catcalls just walking in the streets. 99%. And one wonders: how? Why? What?

There is no question in my mind, there is no question, that that statistic did not exist for the bulk of human history. There is no question that for most of humanity, a woman walking down the street is not going to get grabbed or touched or groped or poked. And yet, 99% in a Muslim land. And I'm telling you, dear brothers, you think that it's not happening with your own family members? Speak to them.

Why am I saying this? Because I need you to understand: you think it's not happening, you think it doesn't exist, but it does exist, and it exists under our very noses. And it is our own daughters and our own wives and our own sisters and our own mothers and our own aunts; they're the ones that are getting all of this. And who's doing it? Collectively, we are, as a society. It's an open secret. We cannot be quiet about this. We have to collectively come together and start manning up, policing our own, making sure our young men are taught. Who's doing all of this groping? Who's doing all of this raping? It's our own men. It's not some foreigners, it's not some invasion. It's our own youngsters, being raised amongst us, coming to our masajid. If we are not going to speak out, if we're not going to teach them, if we're not going to be blunt and frank about this reality, and if we keep on ignoring it because it's taboo and whatnot, how are we going to solve this problem?

Here in America, they did a survey. And again, unfortunately, many Muslim lands don't do these types of surveys the way that they should, because they think it's taboo, and I understand they think it's taboo. Thinking it's taboo is not going to change the situation. In America, three out of five children, three out of five children, reported that some type of molestation happened to them. Do you understand? Three out of five! A'udhu billah, how can this be happening? And unfortunately, in the majority of these cases, who is the one who molests them? It's not some stranger on the street that comes and grabs them or pokes them. No, it is a family friend or a relative. And I'm sorry to be so blunt, but somebody has to speak up; somebody has to call a spade a spade. The guiltiest culprits are typically your own family and friends.

And I'm not telling you to go berserk and suspicious on everybody. I'm telling you to take reasonable precautions. I'm telling you that you need to monitor your own family. I'm telling you, especially those that deal with young children, the parents here, that you need to teach them. You need to teach them at a very young age what is and isn't allowed. And if a young child comes and tells you that somebody is doing something, chances are... again, not 100%, but 99%, chances are... I mean, a six-year-old does not lie. A five-year-old does not know what sexual molestation is, for them to come and tell you that they're feeling uncomfortable, that this is happening and whatnot. And there are ways to extract information; go to a child psychologist and whatnot.

But my point is, dear parents, wallahi, we live in evil times, we live in dangerous times. You need to teach your children, both girls and boys; you need to teach them how to act, how to be dignified, what is and isn't allowed. You need to teach them the realities of our faith. You need to teach them haya and decency. We are surrounded by filth and fahishah and fitnah and fasad.

Yesterday I put a post on Facebook about this latest movie by Netflix about these young girls and, a'udhu billah, suggestive dancing and whatnot. And I have a long post; whoever's watching the video (this is September of 2020), you can look at my Facebook post there and see what I posted about this movie, Cuties or something, from Netflix. A'udhu billah, we are literally destroying our haya, and we are now reaping the consequences of that.

Now, again, these two are separate points here. It doesn't matter how much fahishah is taking place; it does not absolve the responsibility of the rapist.

In any case, I have spoken quite a lot. I need to finish up this question. Actually, the question was about the punishment. And the punishment is very clear here, and that is that no matter what else is going on outside, the rapist, in the end of the day, is responsible. Doesn't matter how much pornography, doesn't matter how she was dressed, doesn't matter what you thought was provocative. All of this, whether it's a crime or not, that's between her and Allah, society and Allah, whatnot. You, as the perpetrator, are guilty for doing a crime, and you have to pay the consequences for that.

And again, a lot can be said, but in a nutshell: in our Shari'ah, somebody who commits this type of crime of holding... you know, this is now in public: she was in public, her car is out of gas, they pull a gun out and whatnot. This type of crime is called hirabah. And hirabah, I mean, they translate it as highway robbery. Hirabah isn't just highway robbery. Hirabah is to break the safety of society. **And rape is a type of hirabah, especially when it is done in the manner that it was done.**

And the Qur'an is very clear about the punishment of hirabah. Listen to this: Surat Al-Ma'idah, verse 33, look it up. Surat Al-Ma'idah, verse 33: "The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger, and who spread evil and corruption on this earth..." And this is what hirabah is. They're spreading evil. This is what hirabah is. You hold up a lady at gunpoint and you rape her in front of her kids: this is hirabah. If this is not hirabah, what is hirabah going to be? The penalty for those who do hirabah is:

1. They be killed.
2. They be crucified.
3. Their hands and their feet be cut off on alternate sides. So if you cut the left hand, you cut off the right, so that it's a marker for as long as the person lives.
4. Or they be negated or denied: they be sent into exile from the land that they're in.

Allah mentions four things. And our scholars mention that the ruler, the judge, the court can look at the case and then decide based upon this.

So hirabah are crimes that threaten social and societal order. And generally speaking, they are crimes that are forced upon somebody. If somebody were to be operating a mafia gang, this is hirabah. If somebody's having a checkpoint where they steal from people when they cross a particular... that's hirabah. Gang rapes of this nature, that's hirabah.

Now, interestingly enough, Imam Malik, Imam al-Awza'i, Imam Abu Hanifah, the Hanafi madhhab, Imam Abu Yusuf, they actually said (and this is their interpretation; the Hanbalis and Shafi'is didn't agree), they said that this verse means... listen to this, a lot of Muslims don't know: this is Islamic law according to these 'ulama, that you are allowed to crucify these people in public and kill them. Now, what does crucify mean? Crucify does not mean you put them on a cross. Crucify means you put their bodies on a pole, and you then kill them in public on a pole, and you leave the body there for everybody to see that this is the man who caused that rape, this is the man who killed that family and children, and this is the man that did that. You want to send the message to society.

Islamic punishments are very different than Western punishments. The whole Western system of punishment is a dismal failure. Look at the American penal system. It is one of the most dismal failures of this country: completely corrupt, completely... it's a money-making scam, which we don't have time to get into here. It does nothing other than spend our taxpayer money and then treat people in the most inhumane manner for the most trivial of crimes. Islamic punishments, Islamic law, make so much more sense, because one of the goals of Islamic punishment is preventative. It is shock and awe. You want to send the message: nobody should do this.

You are allowed, according to Imam Malik, according to the Hanafi madhhab, you are allowed to take this rapist and put him on a stake or a peg so that everybody knows this is the man who did this. Let him be tortured to a certain extent, and then kill him on that stake, and leave that body there for a period of time so that everybody knows this is going to happen. And then, of course, you give him the burial. The other two madhhabs said that you kill him and then you put the body on a stake. So the difference is about when the killing should be done. The Hanafis and Malikis say that you may put him alive on the stake, basically: put him alive there, and then you kill him on that stake, and then leave the body there. And the other two madhhabs say that, well, you're supposed to execute or kill him and then put his body, the corpse, up so that people see.

And again, my teacher Shaykh Ibn 'Uthaymin would say this goes on a case-by-case basis; both are allowed, depending on the severity. And in this particular case, a'udhu billah, in front of the children and on a public highway and whatnot, and all of these things, a'udhu billah, a'udhu billah... I mean, it seems very clear to me that if you're not going to make an example of these people, then what is the purpose of any example here?

So Islam allows a very, very, very harsh penalty, worse than the penalty for murder, because now you are disrupting... Because the penalty for murder is simple execution, just by the sword; you just drop the head off, that's it. These types of crimes, you don't want just a simple execution; you need to send the point across. And so Islam definitely allows this, and it is up to the judge or the federal courts or whatever, if they're judging by the Shari'ah.

As well, the Shari'ah also gives a financial compensation to the victim. And this is dependent on the judge, where the judge will basically decide a financial amount to the victim. So there are two huquq, basically: the haqq of Allah and the haqq of the victim. And the one who does these types of crime, the haqq of Allah is that they be executed by this methodology. Or if it's less than this, if it wasn't rape, something else, maybe the Qur'an says left and right hand side. So, for example, if they did continual highway robbery, a drug dealer, let's say, somebody who's selling drugs to society, it's possible for an Islamic court to say, "We're going to cut off his hand from the right and his foot from the left," so that for the rest of his life... nobody's going to be like that except somebody who's been marked: "Oh, that's the guy who was the drug dealer." Every drug dealer is going to be terrified when they hear of this case.

So the Qur'an actually allows very harsh penalties. And if you ask me, wallahi, it's so common sense. How can anybody make fun of or mock the punishments of the Qur'an? What else are you going to do when somebody does this? You're just going to throw him in an air-conditioned cell for 50 years, feed him five-course meals and let him watch TV and magazines, as most European countries do, or even in America? You're just going to let him live like this? That's not... you need to send the message, and you need to give this point that nobody should be allowed to do this. So that's the haqq of Allah.

And as for the haqq of the lady, or the haqq of the person: a financial compensation that the Shari'ah will mandate, and the courts will decide how much that's going to be. At least something. Of course, the money is not going to bring back what has been taken away, but at least it makes life easier. She's not going to be able to work for a while, et cetera; for a while, she can at least benefit from that. So that is the answer to this.

And in the end of the day, dear brothers and sisters, to conclude on this: wallahi, this is a very sensitive topic. It's a very difficult topic. It's a very emotional topic; even I got a little bit emotional. But wallahi, we need to pull our heads out of the sand. This is a lived reality. As a person who is a member of our community, a shaykh or whatnot, I get bombarded with questions, with personal issues, that make me sick to my core. I get emails from people that tell me what's going on, and it makes you sick to the stomach. How many, especially ladies, but also men, have come to me and told me about what happened to them as a child, and now they're dealing with this as a trauma; they have to deal with it for the rest of their lives.

Really, brothers and sisters, have frank conversations with your immediate family members. Make sure that there's a safe space within the family. Make sure that you can trust one another. Make sure that if anything happens, your children know they can go to you. There are books, there are articles, there are references and guides. Parents especially, do not be naive. Parents, I speak to parents around the globe: you are the number one line of defense after Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. You are the number one. And I speak to normal parents; there is a small percentage, the parents themselves are... typically the man, sometimes. But generally speaking, the parents are the first line of defense.

You have to educate yourself, and you have to then educate your children. And that education starts at a very, very young age, even the age of three or four. You can tell your child, "Nobody should be touching you in your private parts," something like this; "Nobody should do anything like this; if anything happens..." I mean, whatever: you read your culture and your books, because it varies from time to place to culture. But you should be very aware and cognizant, and take as many reasonable precautions as you can, without going too extreme. Because again, you can go too extreme in this regard and start doubting everybody; that's also not good to do.

But do realize that it's a statistical fact that the majority of these molestation and rape cases occur from extended family and from extended friends, because they are the ones that have access to these children and whatnot. Or whether it's even... and again, I'll be honest here, the Qur'an teacher or the Maulvi Sahib or whatnot. Again, these are all things that you need to be careful about. And I'm not asking anybody to doubt every single person. Sometimes the bechara Maulvi Sahib is already under a lot of stress and underpaid, and now you're going to start doubting him, and he's an innocent person. I'm not asking you to do that. I'm just asking: be reasonable. There should never be complete privacy, never complete privacy, between your son or daughter and any other person. It should be in a public space if there's teaching going on. If you send them over to somebody's house to play, make sure you know their environment and whatnot. And all of these things need to be discussed. I cannot dictate your personal preferences, but be aware, be cognizant, speak to your spouse about how you're going to raise your children in this regard, and do whatever you can to spread awareness and to raise the bar of decency and morality.

In the end of the day, Allah 'azza wa jall is the one with whom justice is sought, and the Day of Judgment is where every haqq will be returned to the one it was taken away from, and every dhulm will be answered for. So in case justice is not delivered in this world (we want it to be delivered in this world), in case it is not delivered, we always have the Akhirah to look forward to, on that day. We ask Allah 'azza wa jall to protect ourselves and our loved ones and our families from all evil and fahishah. We ask Allah 'azza wa jall to make sure that these types of crimes are eliminated from our immediate circles. We ask Allah for His 'afiyah and mu'afah in the din and the dunya.
